content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
107	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
108	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
109	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
110	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
111	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
112	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
113	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
114	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
115	the usual `409 conflict`.
116	
117	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
118	hold:
119	
120	```http
121	PUT /quotas
122	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
123	X-Tenant-Id: acme
124	
125	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
126	```
127	
128	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
129	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
130	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
131	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
132	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
133	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
134	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
135	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
136	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
137	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
138	
139	```http
140	GET /quotas
141	X-Tenant-Id: acme
142	```
143	
144	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
145	when the tenant has declared none.
146	
147	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
148	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
149	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
150	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
151	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
152	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
153	
154	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
155	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
156	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
157	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
158	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
159	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
160	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
161	
162	### Usage metering and billing
163	
164	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
165	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
166	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
167	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
168	metered action types are:
169	
170	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
171	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
172	  definition;
173	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
174	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
175	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
176	  `schedule_triggered`;
177	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
178	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
179	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
180	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
181	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
182	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
183	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
184	  meters nothing.
185	
186	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
187	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
188	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
189	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
190	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
191	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
192	
193	```http
194	GET /usage
195	X-Tenant-Id: acme
196	```
197	
198	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
199	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
200	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
201	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
202	
203	```http
204	GET /bill
205	X-Tenant-Id: acme
206	```
207	
208	Returns the per-type bill:
209	
210	```json
211	{"bill":{"items":[
212	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
213	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
214	],"total":2100}}
215	```
216	
217	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
218	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
219	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
220	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
221	
222	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
223	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
224	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`:
225	
226	```http
227	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
228	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
229	X-Tenant-Id: acme
230	```
231	
232	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
233	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
234	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
235	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
236	  as before;
237	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
238	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
239	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
240	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
241	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
242	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
243	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
244	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
245	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
246	  `0`.
247	
248	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
249	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
250	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
251	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
252	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
253	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
254	
255	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
256	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
257	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
258	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
259	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
260	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
261	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
262	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
263	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
264	
265	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
266	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
267	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
268	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
269	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
270	
271	### Per-record usage history
272	
273	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
274	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
275	checked against the moment it occurred:
276	
277	```http
278	GET /usage/records?limit=50
279	X-Tenant-Id: acme
280	```
281	
282	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
283	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
284	sequence. Each record is:
285	
286	```json
287	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
288	```
289	
290	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
291	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
292	  filter or a page;
293	- `type` is the metered action type;
294	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
295	  ending in `Z`.
296	
297	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
298	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
299	like every other JSON endpoint.
300	
301	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
302	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
303	pagination:
304	
305	```http
306	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
307	```
308	
309	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
310	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
311	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
312	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
313	  returned, exactly as before;
314	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
315	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
316	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
317	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
318	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
319	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
320	  contains more than that many records;
321	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
322	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
323	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
324	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
325	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
326	
327	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
328	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
329	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
330	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
331	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
332	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
333	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
334	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
335	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
336	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
337	
338	### Operational metrics
339	
340	```http
341	GET /metrics
342	X-Tenant-Id: acme
343	```
344	
345	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
346	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
347	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
348	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
349	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
350	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
351	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
352	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
353	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
354	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
355	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
356	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
357	
358	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
359	timestamp ending in `Z`:
360	
361	```http
362	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
363	X-Tenant-Id: acme
364	```
365	
366	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
367	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
368	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
369	  counts every recorded fact;
370	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
371	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
372	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
373	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
374	  result.
375	
376	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
377	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
378	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
379	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
380	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
381	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
382	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
383	completion or termination event.
384	
385	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
386	
387	```http
388	GET /metrics/export
389	X-Tenant-Id: acme
390	```
391	
392	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
393	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
394	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
395	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
396	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
397	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
398	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
399	
400	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
401	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
402	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
403	ordered by ascending label value:
404	
405	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
406	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
407	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
408	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
409	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
410	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
411	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
412	  unlabeled scalar samples.
413	
414	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
415	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
416	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
417	ends with a single newline.
418	
419	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
420	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
421	failures, and schedule triggers:
422	
423	```json
424	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
425	```
426	
427	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
428	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
429	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
430	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
431	  ended for that reason.
432	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
433	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
434	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
435	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
436	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
437	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
438	  another attempt, per node identifier.
439	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
440	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
441	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
442	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
443	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
444	
445	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
446	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
447	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
448	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
449	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
450	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.

453	
454	```http
455	GET /health
456	```

460	### Create a workflow
461	
462	```http
463	POST /workflows
464	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
465	
466	{
467	  "id": "order-flow",
468	  "nodes": [
469	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
470	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
471	  ]
472	}
473	```
474	
475	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
476	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
477	
478	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
479	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
480	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
481	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
482	
483	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
484	
485	```json
486	{
487	  "id": "order-flow",
488	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
489	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
490	}
491	```
492	
493	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
494	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
495	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
496	
497	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
498	
499	```json
500	{
501	  "id": "nightly-orders",
502	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
503	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
504	}
505	```
506	
507	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
508	
509	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
510	
511	```json
512	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
513	```
514	
515	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
516	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
517	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
518	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
519	`false`.
520	
521	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
522	
523	```json
524	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
525	```
526	
527	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
528	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
529	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
530	dependencies of its successors.
531	
532	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
533	
534	```json
535	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
536	```
537	
538	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
539	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
540	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
541	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
542	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
543	`retries_exhausted`.
544	
545	A task may instead declare an approval point:
546	
547	```json
548	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
549	```
550	
551	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
552	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
553	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
554	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
555	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
556	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
557	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
558	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
559	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
560	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
561	move the task.
562	
563	### Submit an approval decision
564	
565	```http
566	POST /executions/run-1/decision
567	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
568	
569	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
570	```
571	
572	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
573	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
574	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
575	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
576	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
577	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
578	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
579	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
580	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
581	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
582	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
583	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
584	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
585	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
586	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
587	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
588	404.
589	
590	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
591	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
592	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
593	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
594	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
595	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
596	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
597	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
598	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
599	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
600	shape and event stream.
601	
602	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
603	segment:
604	
605	```json
606	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
607	```
608	
609	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
610	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
611	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
612	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
613	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
614	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
615	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
616	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
617	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
618	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
619	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
620	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
621	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
622	loop node instead).
623	
624	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
625	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
626	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
627	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
628	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
629	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
630	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
631	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
632	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
633	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
634	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
635	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
636	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
637	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
638	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
639	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
640	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
641	belong only to their iterations.
642	
643	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
644	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
645	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
646	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
647	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
648	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
649	exactly.
650	
651	### Dynamic map nodes
652	
653	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
654	recorded array:
655	
656	```json
657	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
658	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
659	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
660	```
661	
662	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
663	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
664	
665	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
666	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
667	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
668	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
669	  the same path syntax as a condition.
670	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
671	  expand.
672	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
673	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
674	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
675	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
676	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
677	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
678	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
679	
680	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
681	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
682	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
683	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
684	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
685	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
686	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
687	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
688	overwrite another instance.
689	
690	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
691	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
692	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
693	become available in the usual way.
694	
695	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
696	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
697	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
698	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
699	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
700	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
701	
702	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
703	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
704	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
705	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
706	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
707	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
708	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
709	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
710	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
711	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
712	
713	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
714	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
715	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
716	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
717	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
718	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
719	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
720	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
721	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
722	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
723	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
724	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
725	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
726	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
727	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
728	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
729	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
730	
731	### Maps inside loop bodies
732	
733	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
734	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
735	other body member:
736	
737	```json
738	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
739	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
740	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
741	```
742	
743	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
744	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
745	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
746	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
747	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
748	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
749	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
750	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
751	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
752	
753	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
754	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
755	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
756	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
757	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
758	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
759	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
760	influence from the iteration number.
761	
762	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
763	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
764	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
765	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
766	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
767	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
768	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
769	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
770	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
771	
772	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
773	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
774	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
775	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
776	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
777	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
778	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
779	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
780	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
781	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
782	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
783	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
784	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
785	
786	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
787	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
788	
789	### Delete and modify expanded instances
790	
791	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
792	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
793	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
794	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
795	
796	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
797	that has permanently failed:
798	
799	```http
800	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
801	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
802	
803	{}
804	```
805	
806	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
807	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
808	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
809	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
810	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
811	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
812	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
813	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
814	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
815	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
816	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
817	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
818	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
819	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
820	
821	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
822	before it is worked:
823	
824	```http
825	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
826	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
827	
828	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
829	```
830	
831	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
832	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
833	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
834	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
835	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
836	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
837	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
838	is stored verbatim.
839	
840	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
841	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
842	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
843	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
844	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
845	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
846	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
847	
848	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
849	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
850	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
851	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
852	carries no loop context.
853	
854	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
855	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
856	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
857	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
858	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
859	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
860	first result and appends no second event.
861	
862	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
863	
864	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
865	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
866	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
867	  and `iteration`;
868	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
869	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
870	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
871	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
872	
873	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
874	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
875	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
876	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
877	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
878	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
879	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
880	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
881	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
882	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
883	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
884	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
885	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
886	
887	### Re-expand a dynamic node
888	
889	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
890	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
891	
892	```http
893	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
894	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
895	
896	{}
897	```
898	
899	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
900	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
901	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
902	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
903	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
904	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
905	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
906	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
907	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
908	bounds start from zero.
909	
910	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
911	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
912	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
913	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
914	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
915	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
916	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
917	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
918	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
919	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
920	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
921	expansion.
922	
923	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
924	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
925	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
926	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
927	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
928	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
929	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
930	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
931	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
932	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
933	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
934	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
935	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
936	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
937	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
938	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
939	an instance that stayed deleted.

941	### Workflow versions
942	
943	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
944	
945	```json
946	{
947	  "id": "order-flow",
948	  "version": "2026-09-25",
949	  "nodes": [
950	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
951	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
952	  ]
953	}
954	```
955	
956	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
957	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
958	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
959	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
960	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
961	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
962	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
963	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
964	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
965	
966	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
967	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
968	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
969	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
970	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
971	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
972	
973	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
974	current version at the moment it starts:
975	
976	```http
977	POST /executions
978	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
979	
980	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
981	```
982	
983	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
984	
985	```json
986	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
987	```
988	
989	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
990	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
991	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
992	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
993	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
994	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
995	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
996	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
997	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
998	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
999	conclusions never change.
1000	
1001	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
1002	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
1003	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
1004	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1005	stream with no added field.
1006	
1007	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
1008	
1009	```http
1010	GET /workflows/order-flow
1011	```
1012	
1013	```json
1014	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
1015	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
1016	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
1017	]}
1018	```
1019	
1020	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1021	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1022	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1023	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1024	resources as usual.
1025	
1026	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1027	
1028	```http
1029	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
1030	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
1031	
1032	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
1033	```
1034	
1035	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
1036	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
1037	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
1038	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
1039	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
1040	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
1041	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
1042	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
1043	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
1044	carries the target version.
1045	
1046	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
1047	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
1048	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
1049	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
1050	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
1051	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
1052	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
1053	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
1054	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
1055	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
1056	
1057	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
1058	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
1059	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
1060	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
1061	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
1062	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
1063	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
1064	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1065	content.
1066	
1067	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
1068	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
1069	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
1070	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
1071	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1072	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
1073	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
1074	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
1075	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
1076	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
1077	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
1078	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
1079	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
1080	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
1081	
1082	### Start an execution
1083	
1084	```http
1085	POST /executions
1086	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
1087	
1088	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
1089	```
1090	
1091	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
1092	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
1093	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
1094	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
1095	
1096	An execution may declare a timeout:
1097	
1098	```json
1099	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
1100	```
1101	
1102	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
1103	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
1104	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
1105	a timeout never expire.
1106	
1107	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
1108	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
1109	
1110	```json
1111	{
1112	  "id": "run-3",
1113	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1114	  "input": {},
1115	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1116	}
1117	```
1118	
1119	### List workflows
1120	
1121	```http
1122	GET /workflows?limit=50
1123	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1124	```
1125	
1126	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1127	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1128	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1129	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1130	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1131	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1132	state.
1133	
1134	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1135	
1136	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1137	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1138	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1139	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1140	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1141	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1142	  returns the definite empty list.
1143	
1144	### List executions
1145	
1146	```http
1147	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1148	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1149	```
1150	
1151	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1152	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1153	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1154	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1155	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1156	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1157	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1158	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1159	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1160	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1161	change no state or metering conclusion.
1162	
1163	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1164	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1165	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1166	
1167	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1168	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1169	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1170	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1171	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1172	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1173	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1174	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1175	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1176	  `400 validation_error`;
1177	- `since` and `until` — the same closed creation-time bounds the events and
1178	  metrics queries accept: each is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`,
1179	  and an execution whose `created_at` equals `since` or `until` is
1180	  returned. When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is
1181	  open, so omitting both returns exactly the unfiltered list; a malformed
1182	  timestamp is a `400 validation_error`. When `since` is later than
1183	  `until` the window matches nothing and the result is the definite empty
1184	  list, not an error.
1185	
1186	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1187	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1188	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1189	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1190	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1191	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.

1193	### Inspect an execution
1194	
1195	```http
1196	GET /executions/run-1
1197	GET /executions/run-1/events
1198	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1199	```
1200	
1201	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1202	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1203	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1204	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1205	
1206	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1207	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1208	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1209	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1210	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1211	
1212	```http
1213	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1214	```
1215	
1216	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1217	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1218	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1219	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1220	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1221	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1222	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1223	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1224	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1225	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1226	  order.
1227	
1228	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1229	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1230	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1231	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1232	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1233	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1234	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1235	`404 not_found`.

1237	### Webhook notifications
1238	
1239	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1240	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1241	
1242	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1243	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1244	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1245	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1246	  reason);
1247	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1248	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1249	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1250	
1251	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1252	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1253	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1254	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1255	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1256	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1257	subscriptions" below.
1258	
1259	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1260	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1261	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1262	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1263	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1264	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1265	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1266	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1267	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1268	triggered it.
1269	
1270	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1271	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1272	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1273	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1274	results as before.
1275	
1276	### Inspect the delivery history
1277	
1278	```http
1279	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1280	```
1281	
1282	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1283	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1284	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1285	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1286	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1287	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1288	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1289	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1290	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1291	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1292	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1293	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1294	
1295	### Queue subscriptions
1296	
1297	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1298	
1299	```json
1300	{
1301	  "id": "run-4",
1302	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1303	  "input": {},
1304	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1305	}
1306	```
1307	
1308	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1309	
1310	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1311	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
1312	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
1313	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
1314	
1315	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
1316	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
1317	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
1318	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
1319	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
1320	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
1321	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
1322	
1323	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
1324	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
1325	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
1326	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
1327	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
1328	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
1329	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
1330	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
1331	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
1332	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
1333	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
1334	before.
1335	
1336	### Inspect the queue state
1337	
1338	```http
1339	GET /executions/run-4/queues
1340	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1341	```
1342	
1343	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
1344	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
1345	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
1346	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
1347	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
1348	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
1349	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
1350	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
1351	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
1352	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
1353	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
1354	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
1355	
1356	### Pull messages from a queue
1357	
1358	```http
1359	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
1360	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
1361	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1362	
1363	{}
1364	```
1365	
1366	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
1367	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
1368	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
1369	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
1370	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
1371	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
1372	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
1373	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
1374	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1375	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1376	
1377	### Acknowledge a message
1378	
1379	```http
1380	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
1381	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
1382	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1383	
1384	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
1385	```
1386	
1387	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
1388	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
1389	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
1390	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
1391	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
1392	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
1393	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
1394	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
1395	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
1396	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
1397	`conflict`.
1398	
1399	### Schedules
1400	
1401	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
1402	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
1403	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
1404	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
1405	
1406	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
1407	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
1408	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
1409	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
1410	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
1411	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
1412	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
1413	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
1414	
1415	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
1416	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
1417	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
1418	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
1419	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
1420	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
1421	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
1422	created is exposed through the status query below.
1423	
1424	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
1425	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
1426	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
1427	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
1428	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
1429	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
1430	
1431	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
1432	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
1433	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
1434	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
1435	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
1436	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
1437	
1438	### Declare or replace a schedule
